In other words, he must describe the content of the phenomenologist’s consciousness as a phenomenologist.
But the content of that consciousness is nothing other than the Phenomenology itself, since the phenomenologist is its author and, as phenomenologist, nothing more than its author.
The “next” stage of Phenomenology therefore consists in repeating its entire content.
Its end thus returns once more to its beginning.

Through Phenomenology, then, the phenomenologist understands, explains, or deduces himself as the author of the Phenomenology. He shows why the content of his consciousness necessarily belongs to the person he is rather than to someone else.
This is precisely what its circularity consists in.
Here again, however, we must emphasize the difference between Hegel’s Phenomenology and mine.

By understanding himself as a phenomenologist, Hegel found that he could do nothing other than write the Phenomenology and then move from it to the Encyclopaedia—that is, in our terminology, to Philosophy.

When I understand myself in the same way, by contrast, I find myself to be a Marxist-Leninist-Stalinist. For me, alongside the possibility of phenomenological and philosophical knowledge, there still remains the possibility—and indeed the duty—of creative-and-revolutionary sociopolitical activity: the completion of socialism and the laying of the foundations of future communism.
But insofar as I am a phenomenologist, I find myself in the same situation as Hegel.
Within that limit, my Phenomenology is just as circular as his.
Yet this limitation, without destroying the circularity, changes its meaning and importance.
For Hegel, because history had ended, the standpoint of the phenomenologist was in principle absolute.

Reality did not merely “appear” to a consciousness peculiar to the phenomenologist—that is, a consciousness characteristic of his historical age—nor was reality mediated by a form of knowledge that existed only for him.
Reality was supposedly given to him as it truly is.
The Marxist phenomenologist, by contrast, knows that even under fully realized socialism a socialist ideology still prevails, whereas the “true” reveals itself completely only under communism.
In other words, he knows that reality appears to him only in a specifically socialist form.
This means that the end of his Phenomenology is not the end of the definitive Phenomenology.
It is not the final end of the dialectical development of phenomena, or of the ways in which world and humanity appear to human beings.
The reason is simply that human beings themselves are still changing as they pass from socialism to communism.

Even so, the end of a “socialist” Phenomenology is just as necessary and just as much “in the nature of things” as the end of a “communist” Phenomenology, or of the genuinely definitive and fully true Phenomenology.
Once the phenomenologist reaches his own standpoint, he obviously cannot go beyond it.
He must therefore bring his phenomenological description to an end by describing that standpoint—which means, in effect, repeating his own Phenomenology.
In this sense, then, it remains circular.
Phenomenology is circular above all because it eventually reaches the point at which it describes itself and therefore begins to repeat itself.
In this respect, we can say that it is circular in the same way as every complete autobiography.
A genuinely complete autobiography should in principle end with the words:
And to understand fully what that sentence means, one must read the autobiography again.
Only then will we know exactly what the author is doing “now.”
The difference is that an ordinary, non-philosophical autobiography does not demonstrate the necessity of its own being written.
We learn that the author did in fact write it, but we do not see that the author necessarily had to write it.

Phenomenology, by contrast, shows that “now” human beings can in principle do nothing other than write a Phenomenology—at least if they wish to “do” something essentially new, something that did not already exist.
A philosophical or phenomenological autobiography—a Phenomenology—therefore differs from a literary autobiography through its necessity and universality, and hence through its truth.
Yet, as we have seen, all this applies only to the definitive, “communist” Phenomenology.
The author of a “socialist” Phenomenology could have chosen not to write it and done something else instead—even something essentially new—namely, begun building communism.
But if that is so, if writing a Phenomenology is neither “necessary nor universal,” then that Phenomenology is not absolutely true.
The guarantee provided by this kind of circularity is therefore insufficient.
It shows that a Phenomenology written by a particular author cannot be more complete than it already is.
But it does not guarantee that another author living in the same historical period could not go beyond that completeness.
In other words, nothing guarantees that this circularity is not merely subjective.
A particular author may simply have exhausted his own capacity for understanding, without thereby exhausting all the objective possibilities of understanding available at that historical moment.
So as long as the historical process itself remains unfinished—as the Phenomenology itself shows—this “subjective” circularity cannot serve as a sufficient criterion of its truth.
Fortunately, however, there is also an objective circularity. And this is found not only in the definitive Phenomenology, but in ours as well.

As I have already said, “sensation” is the starting point of the phenomenological description. So if the Phenomenology is to be circular, it must return to this same sensation when it reaches its end.
And that is exactly what happens.

The phenomenologist begins with a consciousness whose entire content consists in sensation and eventually arrives at his own consciousness. There he discovers his desire to write a Phenomenology. But this desire is specifically a desire to write it and to publish it as a book so that other people can read it.
And since a book can be read only through some form of sensation, the Phenomenology, at its end, sends us back to its beginning.

To understand what the book called Phenomenology is, we must begin by understanding the sensation through which the book “appears” to a consciousness. And that sensation must be understood in exactly the way the Phenomenology understands it at the beginning. For the Phenomenology shows how, starting from an initial sensation of actual reality, consciousness eventually produces this meaningful book.

So we must understand how sensing the physical appearance of the book leads us to understand its meaning. In other words, how does this sensation lead the reader’s consciousness to reproduce the book in the same way that the author’s consciousness “produced” it?

In both cases we begin with the same content of consciousness—the sensation of material actuality, which may include, for example, the space occupied by this book—and arrive at the same content: the meaning of the Phenomenology.
We therefore genuinely repeat the movement of the Phenomenology. In that sense, it really is circular.
At first sight, this kind of circularity may seem trivial and unconvincing. After all, almost every philosopher has published books, and that certainly does not prove that those books are true.

But we must not forget that the essential point is not simply that the Phenomenology happens to exist as a book. The essential point is that the Phenomenology itself shows why it is necessary for it to exist in this form.
This kind of “derivation” of the book’s material existence from its meaning appears for the first time in Hegel’s Phenomenology—and it is repeated in ours.

Earlier philosophers often wrote and published their works. But they never regarded publication as something required by philosophy itself, or believed that the truth of their philosophy depended on it.

The classical “sage,” on the contrary, is not supposed to concern himself with other people, still less with what they think of him or of his thought. He is “his own judge.” He discovers truth in solitude and knows that the truth does not depend on whether he communicates it to anyone else. If he does share it, he does so only out of compassion for human ignorance or for some other reason external to philosophy.
Hegel, by contrast, was the first to understand that only social recognition can guarantee the “normality” and the historical relevance of thought, including philosophical thought.

I can know that I am not insane, and that my Phenomenology is not simply the delirium of a madman, only because other people “recognize” it in one way or another—even if they recognize it only as something “worth discussing.”

Without this guarantee of “normality,” no kind of circularity could guarantee truth. Normality may not be enough for truth, but it remains an absolutely necessary condition of truth and of the search for it.
But circularity also presupposes social recognition in another sense.

The Phenomenology is circular only because it describes itself as a certain “manifestation” of its historical period. Yet the phenomenologist can know this only because his period “recognizes” his book. Only that recognition shows him that his Phenomenology genuinely belongs to its time, since it reveals the book as a product of “its age.” That is what allows it to count as a particular “dialectical stage.”
So the “circularity” of the Phenomenology presupposes—and, so to speak, includes—its being “socially recognized.”
Only the circularity of a book recognized by its age guarantees genuine circularity.

But such recognition is obviously impossible unless the book is written and read. The Phenomenology can therefore be circular only if, when it speaks about itself, it also explains how and why it is read and understood.
And that means precisely that when it reaches its end, it returns to its beginning—to “sensation”—and begins again from there.
In other words, the Phenomenology is circular, and therefore true, only because it includes the idea that it must be socially recognized.
That is still something genuinely new, and far from trivial.
And it is clear that this kind of circularity is no longer subjective but objective.

The first kind of circularity ultimately takes us only to the author’s point of view—the “for us”—from which the book was written from the very beginning and from which all its descriptions of its object are made.
In this sense, we can say that the beginning of the Phenomenology is also its end.
But this shows only that the author has exhausted all of his own subjective possibilities.
The second kind of circularity, by contrast, takes us back to the object itself described at the beginning: sensation.
In this sense, we can say that the end of the Phenomenology is also its beginning.

And this shows that the objective possibilities of the object itself have also, so to speak, been exhausted. It means not merely that this particular author can go no further, but that no one else can either.
Put briefly, the second kind of circularity guarantees the universality and necessity of the Phenomenology—that is, its truth.
At first sight, this may seem to contradict what I said earlier about the definitive or “communist” Phenomenology in relation to our present, “socialist” one.
But there is really no contradiction, for the following reason.
If the communist Phenomenology is the last one, then the socialist Phenomenology must be the next-to-last.

Admittedly, when I describe my own Phenomenology in this way, I am getting somewhat ahead of events. I am treating it as though it were being written at the end of the socialist period, when socialism has been completely realized and firmly established throughout the world.
In fact, of course, this is not yet the case.

But by accepting this fiction, we do not violate the basic principles of dialectical thought. Such an “anticipation” is legitimate if the expected development follows “the order of things” and amounts to the completion of something already given and already present in actuality.

And from Stalinist actuality, one can undoubtedly maintain that the further course of history will not consist in the emergence of some new social and political system outside the USSR. It will consist instead in the spread of the Stalinist-Soviet system across the entire planet.
My anticipation is therefore, if you like, simply an “idealization” of actuality—the kind of idealization that phenomenological description has always used.
By “getting ahead of myself,” I nevertheless remain within the same historical age, which already genuinely exists, and therefore within the same dialectical stage.
And understanding this age shows that it can be followed—and immediately followed—only by the age called “communist.”

For a dialectical understanding of a given period reveals the dialectical character of the period that must follow it. If, for example, the present stage is an antithesis, the next will be a synthesis, and so on.

As we will see later, our socialist age can be shown to be synthetic—that is, to function as a thesis in relation to the period that follows it. The next period can therefore only be its negation in the sense of a “dialectical overcoming.”
And in Marxism, the “dialectical overcoming” of socialism is called communism.
So we must say that the socialist Phenomenology is the next-to-last one.
But from another point of view, we can also say that it is the “last,” and therefore “definitive.”
As we will see, socialism is the final properly historical synthesis.
In other words, its “dialectical overcoming” in communism also means the “overcoming” of history as such.
History—that is, the social and political, or if you prefer collective, process through which humanity develops—ends with socialism.
Society as society and the state as state reach their definitive forms there. The human collective as such will no longer change.
In what follows socialism—that is, in communism—creative development will no longer be collective but individual.
Because under socialism the individual will finally and completely become one with society in the widest sense—with humanity as a whole.
In other words, the individual’s “interests” will no longer differ from humanity’s interests.
